name: Mayor's office
role: Introduces ordinances to Council, appoints the Plan Commission and the DPD commissioner, and sets the agenda for major deals. Mayor Johnson introduced the $424.9M TIF amendment for The 78 on June 17, 2026.
summary: Proposed the 2026 TIF amendment that reimburses the developer for streets, Metra track work, the river wall and a city-owned garage.
quote: "All of that is being worked through." (on TIF details, Mar 2026)

name: Senior mayoral adviser (Jason Lee)
role: Senior adviser in the mayor's office who spoke publicly for the TIF package.
summary: Defended the city-owned garage as a platform that could later carry housing and towers above it.

name: Dept. of Planning and Development
role: Reviews the PD application, negotiates the redevelopment agreement and later reviews each phase's site plan.
summary: Presented The 78 PD 1434 amendment to the Plan Commission (Commissioner Ciere Boatright).

name: Chicago Plan Commission
role: Mayor-appointed board that reviews planned developments before City Council.
summary: Heard and advanced the PD 1434 amendment on Sep 18, 2025 and received the written comments.
source: Plan Commission hearing deck, Sep 18 2025; MPC Zine on Zoning

name: City Council and Zoning Committee
role: Holds the final vote on the PD and on the TIF agreement.
summary: Approved the revised PD in 2025 and the $424.9M TIF amendment on Jul 15, 2026 by a wide margin.

name: Ald. Pat Dowell, Ward 3
role: Alderperson for the ward that contains the site. Under aldermanic prerogative, Council and city bodies follow her lead on it.
summary: Called the plan well received, with open questions on pedestrian access, traffic and how TIF money is used.
quote: "There are still some details that need to be worked out related to pedestrian access from the southern end of the site and real clarity on traffic impacts."

name: Ald. Nicole Lee, Ward 11
role: Alderperson for Chinatown and Bridgeport.
summary: Met with the developer and Chinatown leaders (Aug 21, 2025). Acknowledged constituent concerns but did not commit to a CBA.
quote: The city seeks "a balance between growth and sustainability."
source: Borderless, Mar 3 2026; hearing deck outreach list

name: Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez, Ward 25
role: Alderperson for Pilsen (Lower West Side).
summary: The only alderperson to vote against both parts of the 2026 TIF package. Asked for more community feedback before approval.

name: Cook County Assessor
role: Sets the property values that decide how much tax increment the TIF collects.
summary: Never acts on The 78 directly, but its valuations drive the money flow.

name: Overlapping taxing bodies (CPS, Park District, others)
role: Receive property tax that the TIF diverts while the district runs.
summary: Bear the cost of the tax increment while the TIF district is active.

name: State of Illinois (TIF Act, state roads)
role: Writes the TIF law and controls state roads near the site.
summary: Sets the rules the city's TIF deal operates under.

name: CTA
role: Transit agency that would have run the 15th/Clark Red Line station.
summary: The $364M station was dropped from the plan in June 2025.

name: Metra and RTA
role: Run the Rock Island tracks through the site.
summary: The $85M track realignment was dropped. The 2026 TIF instead pays for upgrades to the on-site tracks.

name: River permitting agencies
role: State and federal permits for river wall and riverbank work.
summary: Must sign off on the river edge work.

name: Chicago Park District
role: Owns and runs Ping Tom Memorial Park next to the site.
summary: Neighbors the site and may take on new open space.

name: Related Midwest (Roosevelt/Clark Partners)
role: Master developer that controls the 62-acre site and is the PD applicant.
summary: Reimbursed up to $424.9M in TIF for infrastructure. Dropped the Red Line station and the Metra realignment from the plan.
quote: "We know that happens by listening to and working closely with our neighbors every step of the way." (Curt Bailey)
source: Hearing deck, Sep 2025; Crain's, Aug 2025; DPD release, Jul 2026

name: Chicago Fire FC / Joe Mansueto
role: Bought about 10 acres from Related and is privately financing the 22,000-seat stadium.
summary: Stadium broke ground in spring 2026, aiming to open in 2028.

name: Chicago UNIDOS in Construction
role: Coalition of Latino construction firms and workers.
summary: Submitted supporting letters and asked for full inclusion of minority-owned firms.

name: Labor unions and trades
role: Construction labor that would build the project.
summary: Placeholder for organized labor's interest in the construction jobs.

name: Chinatown Chamber of Commerce
role: Business association for Chinatown.
summary: Field research suggests it backs the project for the foot traffic it could bring.

name: Outside chain capital
role: Outside investors and chains buying into Chinatown commercial property.
summary: Field research describes rising outside purchases of storefront property.

name: Metropolitan Planning Council
role: Civic think tank on land use, housing and transportation.
summary: Its 2026 Zoning Assessment criticizes aldermanic prerogative, under which city bodies defer to the local alderperson.

name: South Loop Neighbors
role: Neighborhood association, mostly homeowners.
summary: Board supports the plan provided traffic, transit and pedestrian concerns are addressed.
quote: "Looking forward to ironing out the concerns to make this development an asset." (Jim Wales)

name: Near South Planning Board
role: Community planning nonprofit for the Near South Side.
summary: Sent a letter of strong support to the Plan Commission.
quote: "NSPB strongly supports this ambitious, multi-phased, mixed-use development."

name: Coalition for a Better Chinese American Community (CBCAC)
role: Chinatown community organization that has tracked The 78 since the 2018 land sale.
summary: Leads the push for a legally binding CBA. Signed the Friends of the Chicago River letter.
source: Borderless, Mar 2026; CBCAC site; FoCR letter

name: CBA for The 78 Coalition
role: Coalition (CBCAC, Lugenia Burns Hope Center, People Matter and others) seeking an ordinance with a binding CBA.
summary: Asked Council to slow down before the July 2026 TIF vote and is pushing for affordable housing, local jobs, safe streets and oversight.

name: Ping Tom Park Advisory Council
role: Volunteer council for Ping Tom Memorial Park.
summary: Co-signed the river edge objection and backs the CBA push.

name: Lugenia Burns Hope Center
role: Bronzeville community organizing center.
summary: Part of the CBA coalition.

name: Friends of the Chicago River
role: River advocacy nonprofit.
summary: Objected to cutting the river setback from 100 ft to 30 ft and to seawall along more than half the edge.
quote: "Reducing the river edge setback from 100 feet in the original master plan to the minimum of 30 feet."
source: FoCR letter to Plan Commission, Sep 2025

name: Chinatown land trust initiative
role: Proposed community land trust to take Chinatown parcels off the speculative market.
summary: Mentioned in field research only. No public record found as of Oct 2026, so who leads it and how far along it is remain unconfirmed.

name: "Hit PAUSE" form-letter campaign
role: 16 identical emails to the Plan Commission asking for a pause, a CBA with Chinatown and restored transit. Some came from outside the area.
summary: Speaks about Chinatown's concerns without a mandate from Chinatown groups.

name: Chinatown (Armour Square)
role: Chinatown is not one voice. Expand this node to see its segments.
summary: Owners, tenants, newer owners, outside capital and senior renters stand to gain or lose differently.

name: Legacy Cantonese owner-operators
role: Long-time business and property owners.
summary: Rising land values benefit them when they sell, but traffic and competition hurt their businesses.

name: Chinatown tenant businesses
role: Businesses that rent their storefronts.
summary: Exposed to rent increases and new competition.

name: Newer Mandarin-speaking owners
role: More recent property and business owners.
summary: Field research suggests their interests differ from the legacy owners'.

name: Chinatown senior renters
role: Older, often linguistically isolated renters.
summary: The group most exposed to rising rents and weekend traffic.

name: Bridgeport homeowners
role: Homeowners south of Chinatown.
summary: Worried about traffic, parking and property taxes.

name: Pilsen groups
role: Community groups on the Lower West Side.
summary: Placeholder. The CBA coalition names Pilsen as at risk of displacement.

name: PD 1434 ordinance
role: The planned development ordinance that sets what can be built and the required process.
summary: Amended in 2025 to Waterway Residential-Business Entertainment and Spectator Sports PD 1434.

name: Roosevelt/Clark TIF district
role: Tax increment district that funds the reimbursements, including funds moved over from Canal/Congress.
summary: Pays up to $424.9M to the developer as each phase is built.

name: Public infrastructure agreement (RDA)
role: Contract setting what the TIF reimburses.
summary: Adopted 2019 (up to $453.7M), amended 2022, and amended again Jul 15, 2026 (up to $424.9M).

name: The stadium
role: 22,000-seat privately financed soccer stadium.
summary: Draws event traffic. Written comments expect Wentworth Ave to become the default route in and out.

name: City-owned garage (~1,200 spaces)
role: Below-grade parking structure paid for by the TIF and owned and run by the city.
summary: Approved in the July 2026 TIF amendment.

name: River edge
role: The deteriorated South Branch edge along the site.
summary: Setback cut from 100 ft to 30–40 ft. The TIF pays for river wall work.

name: Rock Island tracks
role: Metra tracks that cut through the site.
summary: Realignment dropped. Upgrades are funded instead.

name: Scrapped Red Line station
role: Planned 15th/Clark CTA station ($364M).
summary: Dropped in June 2025. A top concern in the South Loop survey and the form letters.

name: South Loop survey (n≈653)
role: Online survey of South Loop residents, about three quarters of them homeowners.
summary: 73% supportive. Dowell said it mirrored the feedback she was hearing.
